content.thinking:
This narrative leans into personal warmth and honesty, emphasizing the scientist's values and care for people, which should lift benevolence and integrity impressions strongly. There's some risk that the foreign background and value-laden language could read as advocacy to skeptics, but disclosing personal motives tends to build trust overall.

I'm now working through estimates across the trust dimensions, communication/advocacy role, institutional trust, belief and concern about climate, policy support, and behavioral intentions, along with smaller effects on donation and newsletter signup — settling on non-round figures for each before finalizing.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: This arm is a first-person narrative in which a named oceanographer discloses his motives and values (care for the ocean, people, honesty, inclusivity 'regardless of background or belief'). Its most proximal target is the benevolence/integrity/openness dimensions of trust, and narrative self-disclosure carries a small immediate advantage (~d 0.1–0.2) over dry expository text, so I place the multidimensional trust ATE near the upper-middle of the expected +0.5 to +3.5 band (~+2.3), with a smaller effect on the pre-anchored single trust item and a modest reduction in distrust (distrust items are stickier and partly partisan-identity driven). Because the text also contains vivid impact content (marine heat waves, coastal flooding, vulnerable populations) and an explicit 'deeply concerning' framing, I allow a small positive effect on concern (~+1.3), slightly larger than on belief, which is anchored by pre-measurement and near ceiling for most respondents. His stated goal of sharing evidence so 'everyone can take part' directly legitimizes the communication/engagement role of scientists, so policy_role gets an above-average distal effect (~+1.6), while institutional trust is diluted by the federal-government item and by the messenger being a foreign university scientist. Policy and behavioral intention outcomes are distal and get sub-1-point effects; incentivized behaviors get only a few cents and about a point of sign-up, consistent with megastudy evidence that attitude movement rarely translates into costly action. A minor countervailing risk (value-laden advocacy language could read as bias to skeptics) keeps me from forecasting the top of the range.
